title: Multi-query coalescence samplepad
body:
Objective:
Explore the practical latency vs throughput tradeoffs when applying a small coalescing window across many short, independent queries. This was motivated by many client apps issuing 1-8 token prompts concurrently; hypothesis is that short coalescing can reduce per-request GPU kernel overhead and improve aggregated throughput, but may hurt tail latency for single-request interactive flows.

Hypothesis:
1) A 2-8 ms coalescing window will show best cost/throughput gains for medium QPS (50-300 qps) on A100-like nodes.
2) p50 improves noticeably; p99 may degrade at low load because coalescing waits for extra requests.
3) There exists a sweet spot (around 4 ms) that reduces per-token GPU invocation overhead but preserves interactive p99 for the majority of flows.

Setup / environment:
- Date: runs 2025-11-03 to 2025-11-06 (iterative).
- Cluster: Dedicated inference node (A100 80GB equiv), 1 model replica pinned.
- Model: opt-mini-6B-like (approx), quantized to q4_0 for baseline; also one run with fp16 for sanity check. Reported as model: opt-m6b-q4_0.
- Runtime: Redwood serving runtime commit GHPR 4821-built; coalescing feature toggled in request router.
- Client harness: synthetic client (go) generating variable poisson arrivals; max concurrency limiter off; warmup requests separate.
- Measurement window: 5m steady-state after 2m ramp (unless otherwise noted).
- Payloads: 3 payload shapes: tiny (6 tokens), short (24 tokens), medium (120 tokens). Mixed run uses distribution 60% tiny / 30% short / 10% medium.
- Metrics captured: p50, p95, p99 latencies (ms), tokens/s, requests/s, GPU utilization, CPU per-worker, KV cache hit rate (not relevant for independent short prompts), and observed batching sizes.

Coalescing configs tested:
- disabled (0 ms)
- 2 ms
- 4 ms
- 8 ms
- 16 ms (sanity for larger windows)

Key observations (mixed distribution, 150 qps target):
- 0 ms: p50=23ms, p95=72ms, p99=165ms, tokens/s=18.2k, avg batch size=1.07
- 2 ms: p50=18ms, p95=60ms, p99=178ms, tokens/s=21.1k, avg batch size=1.5
- 4 ms: p50=15ms, p95=53ms, p99=185ms, tokens/s=23.7k, avg batch size=1.9
- 8 ms: p50=14ms, p95=57ms, p99=245ms, tokens/s=24.9k, avg batch size=2.6
- 16 ms: p50=13.5ms, p95=84ms, p99=420ms, tokens/s=25.3k, avg batch size=3.1

Interpretation:
- Per-token throughput improved monotonically with window up to 8-16ms, but tail latency (p99) degraded sharply after ~4ms because some lonely requests waited the full coalescing window before being dispatched.
- The p50 gains come from amortizing kernel init/overhead across multiple requests; tokens/s increasing indicates real GPU efficiency wins.
- At 4 ms we get a strong balance: ~30% tokens/s improvement vs baseline while p95 still improves; p99 is slightly worse but within tolerable threshold for many batch-oriented workloads.
- 8ms and 16ms improved throughput slightly more, but the p99 hit is unacceptable for interactive apps.

Single-size microbench (tiny only, 60 qps target):
- 0 ms: p50=10ms, p95=40ms, p99=130ms
- 4 ms: p50=7.8ms, p95=39ms, p99=310ms
Note: p99 blowup is more severe at low overall QPS because fewer concurrent requests available to form batches within the window.

Burst behavior (spiky arrival; 500 qps peak brief 10s):
- coalescing helped smooth GPU load; average batch size spiked to 4.1 during peak for 4 ms.
- transient p99 spikes during ramp-up but recovery was faster because more efficient packing reduced queue buildup.

Edge-case: cold-start + coalescing
- If endpoint is cold (cold kernels / cache warming), coalescing adds small extra delay but total cold latency still dominated by warmup; coalescing did not meaningfully change cold token generation time once kernels loaded.

Telemetry notes:
- Observed requests accumulated in queue for windows >8ms when traffic was sparse. Need to instrument per-tenant lonely-request ratio to guard against p99 harm.
- GPU util improved from 48% -> 72% at 4 ms for mixed distribution run.

Quick conclusions / recommendations:
1) Default coalescing window of 4ms for tenant-class: "compute-efficient" (background batch jobs, low interactivity) yields good unit-cost wins with acceptable tail.
2) Expose policy: per-route override to set coalescing window and a kill-switch for latency-sensitive routes. Suggest route default 0ms for interactive routes and 4ms for batch/ingest endpoints.
3) Add server-side adaptive fallback: if a request waits longer than X ms and current queue length is 0 (i.e., lonely), force immediate dispatch to avoid p99 cliff. Implement small heuristic: if wait_time > 8ms and observed avg concurrency < 1.5 -> flush early.
4) Instrument lonely-request ratio and p99 delta per-tenant. Add alert when p99 increases > 2x after toggling window.
5) For low-QPS single-request flows, avoid static windows >2ms.

Follow-ups / experiments to run next:
- Adaptive windowing: dynamic shrinking of window when queue occupancy low.
- Combine with prefill/priming: if a route has predictable short prompts, prefill KV cache to reduce per-request variance.
- Run across heterogeneous GPU fleet (T4 / A10 / A100 equivalents) to quantify kernel-hookup cost differences.
- Compare with client-side coalescing (grouping at SDK) vs server-side — tradeoffs in fairness and cross-tenant mixing.

Notes to self / TODO:
- Add traces of a few representative lonely-request p99 samples to GHPR for repro.
- Hook new metrics into console (per-route avg batch size, lonely-request ratio).
- Sync with SEs (Marcus) about how this impacts enterprise interactive customers.

Raw logs & commands (high-level):
- harness: ./bench --model opt-m6b-q4_0 --qps 150 --mix tiny:0.6,short:0.3,med:0.1 --coalesce-ms 4 --dur 420
- runtime: docker image redwood/serve:2025-11-01-gh4821
- quick grep on server logs: grep -E "coalesce.*wait=" /var/log/serve/requests.log | head -n 40

Final thought: small, carefully conditioned coalescing is a low-friction lever to improve unit economics for high-volume short-prompt workloads. The trick is policy and telemetry (protect lonely requests).

-- Janelle
